title: Imtiaz Ali Says 'Dhurandhar' Was Called Impractical — Now Everyone Wants to Make It
excerpt: At the HT Leadership Summit, the filmmaker said Bollywood dismissed Aditya Dhar's Ranveer Singh spy thriller as the film least likely to succeed; the franchise has since grossed over Rs 3,000 crore worldwide.
body:
• Filmmaker Imtiaz Ali told the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit on November 14 that Aditya Dhar's Hindi spy thriller Dhurandhar was dismissed inside Bollywood as the "most impractical" film with the "least likelihood of success."
  • The two Dhurandhar films have since grossed over Rs 3,000 crore worldwide between them, according to summit reports — the first film Rs 1,308 crore, the sequel Rs 1,720 crore.
  • Ali's point: the industry is in a phase of introspection about what audiences want, and Dhurandhar "broke all the rules" — after which, he said, everybody wants to make that film.
https://youtube.com/watch?v=BKOVzHcjEIo

One of Bollywood's most successful franchises began as the film the industry was sure would fail. Speaking at the 24th Hindustan Times Leadership Summit on November 14, in conversation with HT's chief managing editor for entertainment and lifestyle Sonal Kalra, filmmaker Imtiaz Ali held up Aditya Dhar's Dhurandhar as proof that conventional box-office wisdom no longer predicts what audiences will turn out for. The project, he said, was initially dismissed by many within the industry as an impractical venture with very little chance of commercial success — in the summit's own framing, the "most impractical" film with the "least likelihood of success."

"The sequel became the first Hindi film to net Rs 100 crore in a single day, and had earned just over Rs 1,025 crore net in India and Rs 1,720 crore worldwide as of April 16."

What Dhurandhar is

Dhurandhar is a Hindi-language spy thriller written and directed by Aditya Dhar, starring Ranveer Singh as an Indian spy operating inside Pakistan, with an ensemble that includes Akshaye Khanna and Sanjay Dutt. The first film released in December 2025 and ran in theatres for over 14 weeks. Its sequel, Dhurandhar: The Revenge, arrived in March 2026. Neither film followed the standard promotional playbook — the franchise's marketing team has separately said it deliberately kept Ranveer Singh away from the usual promotional trail and let the film's material speak for itself.

The numbers that settled the argument

According to the figures cited in summit coverage, the first Dhurandhar collected a then-record Rs 841 crore net in India and, with a $33 million overseas haul — a measure of how strongly the diaspora turned out — crossed Rs 1,300 crore gross worldwide, ending its run at Rs 1,308 crore. The sequel became the first Hindi film to net Rs 100 crore in a single day, and had earned just over Rs 1,025 crore net in India and Rs 1,720 crore worldwide as of April 16. Between them, the two films have grossed over Rs 3,000 crore worldwide, with upper estimates at Rs 3,110 crore. The franchise's cultural footprint is still expanding: Dhurandhar opened the Indian Panorama at IFFI Goa this month.

Why Ali raised it

Ali's remarks were not only about one franchise. He described an industry in a phase of deep introspection, debating the viability of long-form storytelling and whether star power still guarantees an opening — the two assumptions Dhurandhar challenged at once. The irony he pointed to is that a project once considered a risky, non-traditional gamble has become a benchmark other filmmakers now want to emulate: the film broke the rules, and afterwards everybody wanted to make that film. Ali speaks from the other side of the same experience — his own last release, Main Vaapas Aaunga, went on to become a surprise box-office hit. For diaspora audiences, the practical upshot is programming: the commercial case for long, star-led Hindi thrillers that play simultaneously to India and overseas audiences — $33 million of the first film's gross came from outside India — is now the industry's reference point, not its exception.
